extracted.intended_audience: journal editors, publishers, editorial board members, and academic publishing policymakers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and recommended standards for disclosure, prevention, management, and display of editors' conflicts of interest (COIs) in academic journals, including recommended COI form contents, recusal rules, and institutional safeguards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author contributor agreement disclosure requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: In your Journal Publishing Contributor Agreement you will be asked to certify that: 1. All forms of financial support, including pharmaceutical company support, are acknowledged in your Contribution. 2. Any commercial or financial involvements that might present an appearance of a conflict of interest related to the Contribution are disclosed in a covering letter accompanying the Contribution and all such potential conflicts of interest will be discussed with the Editor as to whether disclosure of this information with the published Contribution is to be made in the journal. 3. That you have not signed an agreement with any sponsor of the research reported in the Contribution that prevents you from publishing both positive and negative results or that forbids you from publishing this research without the prior approval of the sponsor. 4. That you have checked the manuscript submission guidelines to see whether the journal requires a Declaration of Conflicting Interests and have complied with the requirements specified where such a policy exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These four explicit certification points are required of authors in the contributor agreement; they cover acknowledgement of financial support, disclosure of commercial/financial involvements in a covering letter, assurance of unrestricted publication rights from sponsors, and compliance with journal-specific COI declaration requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of conflict of interest (COI)
rubrics_metrics.description: “A conflict of interest is a situation in which financial or other personal considerations from authors or reviewers have the potential to compromise or bias professional judgment and objectivity. Authors and reviewers should declare all conflicts of interest relevant to the work under consideration (i.e. relationships, both financial and personal, that might interfere with the interpretation of the work) to avoid the potential for bias.” (Springer definition; similar definitions appear from Taylor & Francis and Wiley).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers' definitions emphasize both financial and personal relationships that might bias interpretation; disclosures should cover relationships that might 'appear to' influence judgment, not only those known to have influenced it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require disclosure of both financial and non-financial COIs
rubrics_metrics.description: COIs in publishing can be divided into two main groups: financial and non-financial. Both types can influence professional judgement. Many journals require that researchers declare financial COIs and an increasing number require non-financial COIs as well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policies should explicitly require disclosure of examples of financial COIs (e.g., business relationships, speaking fees, consulting fees, personal gifts) and non-financial COIs (e.g., personal friendship or enmity, religious beliefs, political convictions, ideological positions, membership of lobbying organizations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Editors must publish regular disclosure statements
rubrics_metrics.description: ICMJE: "Editors who make final decisions about manuscripts should recuse themselves from editorial decisions if they have conflicts of interest ... Editors should publish regular disclosure statements about potential conflicts of interests related to the commitments of journal staff. Guest editors should follow these same procedures."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals should regularly publish institutional or staff-level COI disclosures (e.g., on journal/board webpages or in journal issues) so readers can assess potential influences on editorial decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editor recusal from decisions when COI exists
rubrics_metrics.description: WAME: "(E)ditors should not make any editorial decisions or be involved in the editorial process if they have or a close family member has a COI (financial or otherwise) in a particular manuscript submitted to their journal." ICMJE echoes that editors who make final decisions should recuse themselves when conflicts or relationships pose potential conflicts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recusal includes removing oneself from handling manuscripts from one's own department/institution, collaborators/co-authors (often for a defined period such as past five years), or when personal/political/religious relationships could affect impartiality. When an editor is an author, another editor should manage the manuscript.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanism to reassign manuscripts to non-conflicted editors
rubrics_metrics.description: Elsevier policy considers relationships between the editor, current and recent colleagues, co-authors, and doctoral students as potential COIs; the policy recommends that in such cases manuscripts should be assigned to co-editors, and if none satisfy conflict screens, to the least conflicted co-editor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals should have explicit, pre-established procedures to delegate handling to other editors (including definitions of who counts as conflicted) and to document the reassignment process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content of editorial COI forms / disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: COI forms or statements for editors should include: a complete and updated educational CV, including academic awards, financial compensation, monetary amounts of grants, names of funding agencies, period of research grants, and links between the grant-awarding body and industry; positions on other editorial boards (exact position, journal and publisher name, URL, start and end period, and remuneration or other benefits); positions and membership in academic societies and period of membership; links to industry, companies, or any other non-academic organization, voluntary or remunerated; guest speaker or consultative positions, remuneration, and exact dates of recruitment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forms should be detailed and transparent; the ICMJE provides templates that can be adapted. Disclosures should include remunerated and non-remunerated relationships and provide enough detail (dates, amounts, URLs) to allow assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure timeframe / look-back period
rubrics_metrics.description: The COI forms or statement for editors should not be limited to one or five years back (as suggested by some journals) but should reflect a much longer span (at least ten years) of actual or possible COIs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals should set and state a look-back period for disclosures; the authors recommend at least ten years as more informative than shorter windows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public display of editorial COIs on editor profiles
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors’ profiles should carry a simple PDF file next to their names that displays their professional curricula, including publication lists, expertise, and any links to other groups, publishers, professional societies, journals, or networks—that is, full disclosure of information that would allow academics and the public to decide whether such relationships or positions could be construed as actual or possible COIs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A public, easily accessible COI/CV PDF linked from editorial board pages (using templates such as ICMJE) helps transparency and allows readers to make independent judgements about possible influences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publish corrections/disclosures when COIs are discovered post-publication
rubrics_metrics.description: COPE advises that in cases of COIs coming to light after publication the journal should publish a correction that discloses the COI.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals should have procedures to investigate and, if warranted, publish corrections or notices that disclose previously undisclosed COIs affecting published items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training for editors in recognition and prevention of COIs
rubrics_metrics.description: Not all editors are fully aware of the COIs they bring to their role and there is need for formal training of academic journal editors in methods of recognition and prevention of all forms of COIs. A training cell could be established jointly by WAME, COPE, and ICMJE to provide training to future and current editors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals/publishers should invest in formal COI training programmes for editors and make such training a criterion for editorial appointments or continued service.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid author-suggested peer reviewers to reduce bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Move away from author-suggested peer reviewers, which may be biased, fake or carry COIs, to an editorial system in which editors are exclusively responsible for conducting peer review themselves or for finding and recruiting suitably qualified peers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial policies should limit or vet author-suggested reviewers; editors should recruit independent reviewers and document reviewer selection procedures to reduce biased reviewer selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid abuse of editorial position for personal advantage
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorial failure can include the abuse by editors of their position to either enhance their own work or profiles or to game the metrics system to enhance the metrics of their journal by suggesting excessive citation of their work or of their journal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policies should prohibit coercive/self-serving citation recommendations and establish oversight/enforcement to detect and penalize such behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not create author accounts without explicit permission
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors should not create accounts for authors without their explicit permission first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrative policies should prevent editors or staff from creating or manipulating author profiles/accounts on behalf of authors without consent, as this could be abused.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promote open peer review and public scrutiny where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Open peer review, which discloses the identities of the reviewers as well as their COIs, can allow the entire scientific community a greater chance to give high-quality comments and to point out editorial biases and COIs, though this model has considerable weaknesses and limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals should consider open peer review elements to increase transparency while weighing trade-offs; where used, COIs of reviewers should be declared publicly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require trial registration and reporting guideline endorsement to reduce dissemination bias
rubrics_metrics.description: In medicine, to reduce dissemination bias, clinical trials should be registered and reporting guidelines should be endorsed. Registration helps identify clinical trials and initiation dates, which helps reduce dissemination bias and improper attribution of priority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals, especially in clinical fields, should require trial registration and adherence to reporting standards (e.g., CONSORT), and make registration details publicly visible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish independent ethics/oversight body with enforcement ability
rubrics_metrics.description: An ethics committee with credible representative editors and academicians from various disciplines as members, having enforcement ability that allows them to oversee the adherence of journals to the guidelines set up by COPE, WAME, and ICMJE, should be established; one or more independent watchdogs are required to monitor the 'ethicists' and 'ethical organizations' to avoid ethical exceptionalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers and scholarly societies should support or participate in independent monitoring bodies with powers to investigate, report, and enforce COI policy compliance across journals and organizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specify and publish examples of non-financial COIs to guide disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: PLOS lists non-financial COIs such as: acting as an expert witness; membership in a government or other advisory board; relationship (paid or unpaid) with organizations and funding bodies; membership in lobbying or advocacy organizations; writing or consulting for an educational company; personal relationships with individuals involved in the submission or evaluation; personal convictions (political, religious, ideological) related to a paper’s topic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals should provide explicit examples of non-financial COIs in their policies to help editors, reviewers, and authors recognize and disclose relevant relationships and convictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include COI statements in bibliographic records (e.g., PubMed)
rubrics_metrics.description: The National Library of Medicine (NLM) and the National Institutes of Health (NIH) implemented on March 8, 2017 the inclusion of a COI statement for all entries on PubMed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals and databases should ensure COI statements are included in bibliographic metadata so readers accessing abstracts/listings can view COI information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure alone is insufficient — combine with prevention and management measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Further, disclosure of financial COIs itself is not enough to guarantee the prevention of editorial COIs. Prevention and management of COIs requires a broader approach including transparency, recusal policies, training, oversight, and other structural measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design COI frameworks that combine mandatory disclosure with concrete management steps (recusal, reassignment, public disclosure, training, oversight) rather than relying on disclosure alone.
